plan: New informational essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000006) with a sentence-placement item, who/whom, each-of agreement, and goal-matched relevance; E005-09 resubmitted.

passages.title: Mapping the Dark
passages.text:
When most people imagine cave exploration, they picture squeezing through tight passages in search {{1|for}} undiscovered chambers. The work that occupies most cavers, however, is slower and less glamorous: making maps. {{2|Without a map, a cave that has been explored is, for practical purposes, a cave that has been lost.}}

A survey team usually has three members. The first sets a station—a small numbered marker—at a point the others can see. {{3|The second, who holds a laser rangefinder, measures}} the distance to the station, while the third reads the compass bearing and the slope. {{4|Each of these numbers are recorded}} in a waterproof notebook, along with a sketch of the passage's walls.

[1] Back on the surface, the numbers become a map. [2] A single misread digit can send that path through solid rock. [3] Software converts each set of measurements into a line segment, and the segments, joined end to end, trace the cave's path. [4] For this reason, many teams measure every leg twice, once in each direction.

The work is slow. A team might survey only a few hundred meters in a long day, {{5|and the rangefinders run on rechargeable batteries}}. {{6|Yet}} cavers keep at it, {{7|year after year, decade after decade, for many years}}, because a good map is the one discovery that lasts: {{8|its useful}} to every caver, scientist, and rescue team that enters the cave afterward. {{9|Whom}} else would bother to do it?

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The standard idiom is "in search of."

A.rationale: The idiom is "in search of," not "in search for."

hints: Say the phrase aloud with each preposition.

candidates.subskill: Function of a sentence (what would be lost)
candidates.stem: If the writer deleted the underlined sentence, the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.A: a description of the instruments cavers use to make maps.
choices.B: evidence that most of the world's caves remain unexplored.
choices.C: a transition into the history of cave exploration.
choices.D: an explanation of why the less glamorous work of mapping matters.

candidates.evidence: a cave that has been explored is, for practical purposes, a cave that has been lost
candidates.explanation: The paragraph says mapping is less glamorous; this sentence explains why it matters anyway: without a map, exploration is effectively lost.

A.rationale: Instruments are described in the next paragraph, not here.

B.rationale: The sentence makes no claim about how many caves are unexplored.

C.rationale: The essay never turns to history.

hints: What does the sentence add after "making maps"?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the paragraph would be missing.

candidates.remember: Ask what job a sentence does in its paragraph.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: The second who holds a laser rangefinder, measures
choices.C: The second, who holds a laser rangefinder measures
choices.D: The second who, holds a laser rangefinder, measures

candidates.evidence: while the third reads the compass bearing
candidates.explanation: "Who holds a laser rangefinder" is extra information about "The second" and is set off by a pair of commas.

B.rationale: Without the opening comma, the closing comma wrongly separates the subject from its verb.

C.rationale: The clause opened with a comma must close with one before "measures."

D.rationale: The commas split "who" from its own verb.

hints: Can the clause be removed without losing the sentence's core?

strategy.explanation: Nonessential clauses need commas on both sides.

candidates.remember: Interrupting clauses take a pair of commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Each of these numbers is recorded
choices.C: Each of these numbers were recorded
choices.D: Each of these numbers have been recorded

candidates.evidence: A survey team usually has three members
candidates.explanation: The subject is "Each," which is singular; the passage is in the present tense, so "is recorded."

A.rationale: "Each" is singular, so "are" does not agree.

C.rationale: "Were" is plural and shifts out of the present tense.

strategy.explanation: Ignore the "of" phrase and match the verb to "Each."

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively emphasizes how slow the work is compared with the size of the task?

choices.B: and the team members often take turns at each job
choices.C: and most teams eat lunch underground to save time
choices.D: and some cave systems extend for more than a hundred kilometers

candidates.evidence: A team might survey only a few hundred meters in a long day
candidates.explanation: A few hundred meters a day set against systems over a hundred kilometers long shows how slow the work is relative to the job.

A.rationale: Battery type says nothing about the size of the task.

B.rationale: Rotating jobs does not show the scale of the task.

C.rationale: Lunch habits do not compare speed with scale.

hints: What would make a few hundred meters a day seem slow?

strategy.explanation: The stem names the goal: compare speed with scale.

candidates.remember: Match the choice to the goal in the stem.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: Cavers persist despite the slow work, a contrast: "Yet."

B.rationale: Continuing despite slowness is not a result of the slowness.

C.rationale: Persisting is not similar to the work being slow.

D.rationale: Persisting is not an example of slowness.

hints: Do cavers keep going because of or in spite of the slowness?

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: year after year, for many years

candidates.explanation: "Year after year" conveys the persistence; the other versions repeat it.

A.rationale: "Decade after decade" and "for many years" repeat the same idea.

D.rationale: "Annually" and "year after year" say the same thing.

hints: Which words say the same thing twice?

strategy.explanation: Pick the shortest version that keeps the meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: a good map is the one discovery that lasts
candidates.explanation: The sentence means "it is useful," so the contraction "it's" is needed.

A.rationale: "Its" is possessive; the sentence needs "it is."

D.rationale: "Usefully" is an adverb and cannot follow "is" here.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: else would bother to do it
candidates.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of "would bother," so the subject form "Who" is correct ("He would bother," not "him").

A.rationale: "Whom" is an object form, but the pronoun is the subject of "would bother."

hints: Answer the question with he/him: "___ would bother."
candidates.remember: Use who where he fits; whom where him fits.

candidates.stem: For the sake of the logic and coherence of the third paragraph, Sentence 2 should be placed:
candidates.evidence: A single misread digit can send that path through solid rock.
candidates.explanation: "That path" points back to the path traced in Sentence 3, and Sentence 4's "For this reason" points back to the danger of misread digits. So Sentence 2 belongs between them: after Sentence 3.

A.rationale: "That path" refers to the cave's path, which is not mentioned until Sentence 3.

B.rationale: "That path" would still have nothing to refer to.

D.rationale: Then "For this reason" in Sentence 4 would have no reason before it.

hints: What reason does "For this reason" refer to?

strategy.explanation: Use pointer words (that, this) to order sentences.

candidates.remember: Pointer words must follow what they point to.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to describe how cavers make maps and why they value them. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains the survey process and why maps matter to later visitors.
choices.B: Yes, because it describes the many dangers that cavers face underground.
choices.C: No, because it focuses mainly on the long history of cave exploration.
choices.D: No, because it describes only the equipment that survey teams carry.

candidates.evidence: a good map is the one discovery that lasts
candidates.explanation: The essay walks through the survey method and ends by explaining why maps are valued.

C.rationale: The essay does not discuss history.

D.rationale: It also explains the process and why maps matter.

hints: Does the essay explain both how and why?

strategy.explanation: Decide yes or no, then check the reason.

candidates.remember: Both the verdict and the reason must be right.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: On a Saturday morning in June, Ellison set the hands to the correct time
candidates.explanation: "Began to tick" says it all; the other versions repeat the idea or add a comma error.

A.rationale: "And it was ticking" repeats "began to tick."

D.rationale: A comma should not separate a verb from its infinitive.

hints: Does the extra phrase add any new information?

strategy.explanation: Pick the shortest correct version that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: Cut words that repeat the same idea.
candidates.revision_note: E005-09 resubmitted: the period already follows the underlined span, so the trailing periods were removed from choices B-D (doubled-punctuation check added to qb.py).
